sentences.zh: 詔答曰：「朕不德不明，俾大臣憂疑，朕之過也。朕甚自愧，公勿以為慮。」代宗以子儀頃同患難，收復兩京，禮之逾厚。

translations.literal: The edict replied, "Because I am without virtue and without clarity, I have caused a great minister to be anxious and suspicious. This is my fault. I am deeply ashamed; you, Duke, must not take it as a concern." Because Daizong had recently shared hardship with Ziyi and because Ziyi had recovered the two capitals, the emperor treated him with ever greater honor.
translations.idiomatic: The edict replied, "Because I am without virtue and without clarity, I have caused a great minister to be anxious and suspicious. This is my fault. I am deeply ashamed; you, Duke, must not take it as a concern." Because Daizong had recently shared hardship with Ziyi and because Ziyi had recovered the two capitals, the emperor treated him with ever greater honor.

sentences.zh: 時史朝義尚據洛陽，元帥雍王率師進討，代宗欲以子儀副之，而魚朝恩、程元振亂政，殺裴茂、來瑱，子儀既為所間，其事遂寢，乃留京師。

translations.literal: At that time Shi Chaoyi still held Luoyang; the supreme commander, the Prince of Yong, led an army forward to attack him. Daizong wished to make Ziyi his deputy, but Yu Chao'en and Cheng Yuanzhen misgoverned, killing Pei Mao and Lai Tian; Ziyi having been alienated by them, the matter was shelved, and he remained in the capital.
translations.idiomatic: At the time Shi Chaoyi still held Luoyang, and the Prince of Yong, as supreme commander, marched to attack him. Daizong wished to appoint Ziyi as his deputy, but Yu Chao'en and Cheng Yuanzhen were corrupting the government and had Pei Mao and Lai Tian killed. Ziyi had been turned against, the plan came to nothing, and he remained at court.

sentences.zh: 俄而梁崇義據襄陽叛，僕固懷恩阻兵於汾州，引回紇、吐蕃之眾入寇河西。

translations.literal: Before long Liang Chongyi seized Xiangyang and rebelled; Pugu Huaien held troops in defiance at Fen Prefecture and led Uyghur and Tibetan forces to raid Hexi.
translations.idiomatic: Soon afterward Liang Chongyi seized Xiangyang and rebelled, while Pugu Huaien defied the court with troops at Fen Prefecture and brought Uyghur and Tibetan forces to raid Hexi.

sentences.zh: 明年十月，吐蕃陷涇州，虜刺史高暉，暉遂與蕃軍為鄉導，引賊深入京畿，掠奉天、武功，濟渭而南，緣山而東。

translations.literal: In the tenth month of the following year the Tibetans captured Jing Prefecture and captured the prefect Gao Hui; Hui then served the Tibetan army as a local guide, leading the enemy deep into the capital region, plundering Fengtian and Wugong, crossing the Wei River southward and advancing eastward along the mountains.
translations.idiomatic: In the tenth month of the following year the Tibetans took Jing Prefecture and captured its prefect, Gao Hui. Hui then guided the Tibetan army inland, leading the enemy deep into the capital region. They plundered Fengtian and Wugong, crossed the Wei southward, and marched east along the foothills.

sentences.zh: 渭北行營兵馬使呂日將逆戰於盩厔，自辰至酉，殺蕃軍數千，然其徒多殞。

translations.literal: Lu Rijiang, army-and-horse commissioner of the Weibei field headquarters, met them in battle at Zhouzhi; from the hour chen to the hour you he killed several thousand Tibetan troops, yet many of his own men also perished.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Rijiang, cavalry commander of the Weibei field headquarters, met the invaders at Zhouzhi. From morning until evening he killed several thousand Tibetans, but many of his own men fell as well.

sentences.zh: 賊將逼京師，君上計無所出，遽詔子儀為關內副元帥，出鎮咸陽。

translations.literal: As the enemy generals pressed upon the capital, the sovereign could devise no plan; he urgently appointed Ziyi deputy supreme commander of Guannei and sent him out to take command at Xianyang.
translations.idiomatic: With enemy generals closing on the capital and the emperor at a loss, an urgent edict made Ziyi deputy supreme commander of Guannei and sent him out to hold Xianyang.

sentences.zh: 子儀自相州不利，李光弼代掌兵柄，及征還朝廷，部曲散去。

translations.literal: Since Ziyi had met with misfortune at Xiang Prefecture, Li Guangbi had replaced him in command of the army; when he was recalled to court, his personal followers dispersed.
translations.idiomatic: Ever since his setback at Xiang Prefecture, when Li Guangbi had taken over command, Ziyi's retainers had scattered once he was recalled to court.

sentences.zh: 及是承詔，部下唯二十騎，強取民家畜產以助軍。

translations.literal: When he received this edict, his subordinates numbered only twenty horsemen; he forcibly seized livestock from civilian households to supply the army.
translations.idiomatic: When he answered this summons, only twenty horsemen remained under his command. He forcibly requisitioned livestock from local households to support the army.

sentences.zh: 至咸陽，蕃軍已過渭水。

translations.literal: When he reached Xianyang, the Tibetan army had already crossed the Wei River.
translations.idiomatic: By the time he reached Xianyang, the Tibetan army had already crossed the Wei.

sentences.zh: 其日，天子避狄幸陜州。

translations.literal: That day the Son of Heaven fled the barbarians to Shan Prefecture.
translations.idiomatic: That same day the emperor fled the barbarian advance to Shan Prefecture.

sentences.zh: 子儀聞上避狄，雪涕還京，至則車駕已發。

translations.literal: When Ziyi heard that the emperor had fled the barbarians, he wiped away tears and returned to the capital; when he arrived, the imperial carriage had already departed.
translations.idiomatic: Hearing that the emperor had fled, Ziyi wiped away his tears and hurried back to the capital, but by the time he arrived the imperial procession was already gone.

sentences.zh: 射生將王獻忠從駕，沿路遂以四百騎叛，仍逼豐王已下十王欲投於賊。

translations.literal: The imperial hunt guard Wang Xianzhong accompanied the carriage; along the route he then rebelled with four hundred horsemen and even coerced the ten princes below the Prince of Feng to defect to the enemy.
translations.idiomatic: The imperial hunt guard Wang Xianzhong rode with the procession, but along the way he rebelled with four hundred horsemen and forced ten princes, beginning with the Prince of Feng, toward defection to the enemy.

sentences.zh: 子儀入開遠門，遇之，詰豐王等所向，遂護送行在。

translations.literal: Ziyi entered Kaiyuan Gate, encountered them, questioned the Prince of Feng and the others as to where they were going, and then escorted and sent off the imperial presence.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi entered Kaiyuan Gate, intercepted them, demanded to know where the Prince of Feng and the others were headed, and then escorted the imperial presence on its way.

sentences.zh: 子儀以三千騎傍南山，至商州，得武關防兵及六軍散卒四千人，招輯亡逸，其軍漸振。

translations.literal: Ziyi, with three thousand horsemen along the southern mountains, reached Shang Prefecture; there he obtained the Wuguan garrison troops and four thousand scattered soldiers of the Six Armies, gathered fugitives, and his army gradually revived.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi led three thousand horsemen along the southern slopes to Shang Prefecture, where he gathered the Wuguan garrison and four thousand scattered soldiers from the Six Armies, rallied the fugitives, and gradually restored his force.

sentences.zh: 蕃犯京城，得故邠王守禮子廣武王承宏，立帝號，假署百官。

translations.literal: When the Tibetans violated the capital, they obtained Cheng Hong, Prince of Guangwu, son of the former Prince of Bin Li Shouli; they established an imperial title and provisionally appointed the full roster of officials.
translations.idiomatic: When the Tibetans entered the capital, they found Cheng Hong, Prince of Guangwu, son of the former Prince of Bin, Li Shouli. They set up an imperial regime and provisionally appointed a full bureaucracy.

sentences.zh: 子儀遣六軍兵馬使張知節、烏崇福、羽林軍使長孫全緒等將兵萬人為前鋒，營於韓公堆，盛張旗幟，鼓鞞震山谷。

translations.literal: Ziyi dispatched the Six Armies cavalry commissioners Zhang Zhijie and Wu Chongfu, the Imperial Guard commander Zhangsun Quanxu, and others to lead ten thousand men as the vanguard; they encamped at Han Gongdui, greatly displayed banners and flags, and their drums shook the valleys.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi sent the Six Armies cavalry commissioners Zhang Zhijie and Wu Chongfu, the Imperial Guard commander Zhangsun Quanxu, and others at the head of ten thousand men. They encamped at Han Gongdui, raised a great show of banners, and beat drums that shook the valleys.

sentences.zh: 全緒遣禁軍舊將王甫入長安，陰結少年豪俠以為內應，一日，齊擊鼓於朱雀街，蕃軍惶駭而去。

translations.literal: Quanxu sent the former Imperial Guard general Wang Fu into Chang'an to secretly ally with young gallant men as an inner response; one day they beat drums together in Zhuque Street, and the Tibetan army fled in panic.
translations.idiomatic: Quanxu sent the former Imperial Guard officer Wang Fu into Chang'an to secretly enlist young bravos as inside allies. One day they sounded drums together in Zhuque Street, and the Tibetan army fled in panic.

sentences.zh: 大將李忠義先屯兵苑中，渭北節度使王仲升守朝堂。

translations.literal: The grand general Li Zhongyi first encamped in the imperial park, and Weibei military governor Wang Zhongsheng guarded the audience hall.
translations.idiomatic: Grand general Li Zhongyi first encamped in the imperial park, while Weibei military governor Wang Zhongsheng held the audience hall.

sentences.zh: 子儀以大軍續進，至浐西。

translations.literal: Ziyi continued advancing with the main army and reached the west of the Chan River.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi pressed forward with the main army as far as the west bank of the Chan River.

sentences.zh: 射生將王撫自署為京兆尹，聚兵二千人，擾亂京城，子儀召撫殺之。

translations.literal: The imperial hunt guard Wang Fu self-appointed himself Jingzhao Intendant, gathered two thousand troops, and disturbed the capital; Ziyi summoned Fu and had him killed.
translations.idiomatic: The imperial hunt guard Wang Fu declared himself Jingzhao intendant, raised two thousand men, and threw the capital into disorder. Ziyi summoned him and had him executed.

sentences.zh: 詔子儀權京城留守。

translations.literal: An edict appointed Ziyi provisional Protector of the capital.
translations.idiomatic: An edict appointed Ziyi provisional protector of the capital.

sentences.zh: 自西蕃入寇，車駕東幸，天下皆咎程元振，諫官屢論之。

translations.literal: Since the Western barbarians had invaded and the imperial carriage had gone east, all under Heaven blamed Cheng Yuanzhen, and remonstrating officials repeatedly criticized him.
translations.idiomatic: After the western barbarians invaded and the emperor fled east, the whole empire blamed Cheng Yuanzhen, and censors repeatedly denounced him.

sentences.zh: 元振懼，又以子儀復立功，不欲天子還京，勸帝且都洛陽以避蕃冠，代宗然之，下詔有日。

translations.literal: Yuanzhen grew afraid; moreover, because Ziyi had again won merit, he did not wish the Son of Heaven to return to the capital and advised the emperor to establish the court temporarily at Luoyang to avoid the Tibetan invaders. Daizong agreed, and an edict was to be issued on a set day.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanzhen was afraid, and because Ziyi had distinguished himself again he did not want the emperor to return to Chang'an. He urged Daizong to move the court temporarily to Luoyang to escape the Tibetans. Daizong agreed, and an edict was set to be issued.

sentences.zh: 子儀聞之，因兵部侍郎張重光宣慰回，附章論奏曰：臣聞雍州之地，古稱天府，右探隴、蜀，左扼崤、函，前有終南、太華之險，後有清渭、濁河之固，神明之奧，王者所都。地方數千里，帶甲十餘萬，兵強士勇，雄視八方，有利則出攻，無利則入守。此用武之國，非諸夏所同，秦、漢因之，卒成帝業。其後或處之而泰，去之而亡，前史所書，不唯一姓。及隋氏季末，煬帝南遷，河、洛丘墟，兵戈亂起。高祖唱義，亦先入關，惟能翦滅奸雄，底定區宇。以至於太宗、高宗之盛，中宗、玄宗之明，多在秦川，鮮居東洛。間者羯胡構亂，九服分崩，河北、河南，盡從逆命。然而先帝仗朔方之眾，慶緒奔亡；陛下藉西土之師，朝義就戮。豈唯天道助順，抑亦地形使然，此陛下所知，非臣飾說。近因吐蕃淩逼，鑾駕東巡。蓋以六軍之兵，素非精練，皆市肆屠沽之人，務掛虛名，茍避征賦，及驅以就戰，百無一堪。亦有潛輸貨財，因以求免。又中官掩蔽，庶政多荒。遂令陛下振蕩不安，退居陜服。斯蓋關於委任失所，豈可謂秦地非良者哉！今道路云云，不知信否，咸謂陛下已有成命，將幸洛都。臣熟思其端，未見其利。夫以東周之地，久陷賊中，宮室焚燒，十不存一。百曹荒廢，曾無尺椽，中間畿內，不滿千戶。井邑榛荊，豺狼站嗥，既乏軍儲，又鮮人力，東至鄭、汴，達於徐方，北自覃懷，經於相土，人煙斷絕，千里蕭條。將何以奉萬乘之牲餼，供百官之次舍？矧其土地狹厄，才數百里間，東有成臯，南有二室，險不足恃，適為戰場。陛下奈何棄久安之勢，從至危之策，忽社稷之計，生天下之心。臣雖至愚，竊為陛下不取。且聖旨所慮，豈不以京畿新遭剽掠，田野空虛，恐糧食不充，國用有闕，以臣所見，深謂不然。昔衛文小國之君，諸侯之主耳，遭懿公為狄所滅，始廬於曹，衣大布之衣，冠大帛之冠，元年革車三十乘，季年三百乘，卒能恢復舊業，享無疆之休。況明明天子，躬儉節用，茍能黜素餐之吏，去冗食之官，抑豎刁、易牙之權，任蘧瑗、史䲡之直，薄征馳力，恤隱迨鰥，委諸相以簡賢任能，付老臣以練兵禦侮，則黎元自理，寇盜自平，中興之功，旬月可冀，卜年之期，永永無極矣。願時邁順動，回鑾上都，再造邦家，唯新庶政，奉宗廟以修薦享，謁陵寢以崇孝思，臣雖隕越，死無所恨。

translations.literal: When Ziyi heard of this, he attached a memorial to Zhang Chongguang, Vice Minister of War, as Zhang returned from his consolation mission, and submitted it, saying: Your subject has heard that the land of Yongzhou was called Heaven's storehouse in antiquity. To the right it reaches toward Long and Shu; to the left it controls Xiao and Han. Before it are the defenses of Zhongnan and Taihua; behind it are the fastnesses of the clear Wei and muddy Yellow River. It is a mysterious inner place of divine clarity and the capital of kings. The region extends several thousand li and has more than a hundred thousand armored troops; its soldiers are strong and its men brave, looking proudly over the eight directions. When there is advantage, it goes out to attack; when there is no advantage, it goes in to defend. This is a state for the use of arms and is not the same as the various lands of Xia. Qin and Han relied on it and in the end completed imperial enterprises. Afterward, some who occupied it were secure, and some who left it perished; what earlier histories record is not limited to one surname. By the end of the Sui house, Emperor Yang moved south, the Yellow River and Luo region became mounds and ruins, and wars arose. Gaozu raised the righteous standard and also first entered the Pass, and only then was able to cut down the treacherous heroes and settle the realm. Down to the flourishing of Taizong and Gaozong and the brightness of Zhongzong and Xuanzong, most dwelt in Qinchuan and few lived in Eastern Luo. Recently the Jie barbarian created disorder and the nine services split apart; Hebei and Henan all followed the rebel command. Yet the late emperor relied on the troops of Shuofang, and Qingxu fled in defeat; Your Majesty relied on the armies of the western lands, and Chaoyi was executed. This was not only the Way of Heaven assisting the obedient; it was also the terrain making it so. Your Majesty knows this, and it is not an embellished argument by your subject. Recently, because Tibet pressed and threatened us, the imperial carriage made an eastern tour. This was because the soldiers of the Six Armies had never been well trained; they were all men of the markets, butchers, and sellers of wine, intent on hanging up empty names and merely avoiding conscription and taxes. When driven into battle, not one in a hundred was fit. There were also those who secretly paid money and goods to seek exemption. In addition, eunuchs concealed matters and the many policies were much neglected. This caused Your Majesty to be shaken and unsettled and to withdraw to the region of Shaan. This all relates to appointments being misplaced. How can it be said that the Qin lands are not good? Now there is talk on the roads, and I do not know whether it is trustworthy, but all say Your Majesty already has a settled command and will visit the capital of Luo. Your subject has considered the matter carefully and has not seen its benefit. As for the land of Eastern Zhou, it has long been trapped among the rebels. Palaces and halls have been burned, and not one in ten survives. The hundred offices are desolate and abandoned, without even a foot of beam; in the imperial district between them, there are not a thousand households. Wells and settlements are choked with brush, jackals and wolves howl there, and there is neither military supply nor human strength. Eastward to Zheng and Bian, reaching to Xufang, and northward from Tanhuai, passing through the lands of Xiang, human smoke is cut off and a thousand li are bleak. How will it provide sacrificial animals and provisions for the imperial carriage, or supply lodgings for the hundred officials? Moreover, its territory is narrow, only a few hundred li across. To the east is Chenggao; to the south are the Two Peaks. Its terrain offers no reliable defense and merely makes a battlefield. How can Your Majesty abandon the position of long security, follow a policy of utmost danger, neglect the plan for the altars of state, and produce doubt in the hearts of the realm? Though your subject is extremely foolish, I privately do not choose this for Your Majesty. Moreover, what the sacred intent worries over is surely that the capital region has newly suffered plunder, the fields are empty, grain may not suffice, and state use may have shortages. From what your subject sees, I deeply think this is not so. Formerly Duke Wen of Wei was the ruler of a small state, only a lord among the feudal lords. After Duke Yi was destroyed by the Di, he first lodged at Cao, wore clothes of coarse cloth and a cap of plain silk; in his first year he had thirty war chariots, and by his last year three hundred, and in the end he was able to recover his old enterprise and enjoy boundless blessing. How much more a brilliant Son of Heaven: if you personally practice frugality and economize use, dismiss officials who eat without service, remove redundant food-consuming officers, suppress the power of Shudiao and Yiya, employ the uprightness of Qu Yuan and Shi Qiu, lighten levies and use strength carefully, show compassion to the distressed and reach even widowers, entrust the chief ministers with selecting the worthy and employing the able, and entrust the old minister with training troops and resisting insult, then the black-haired people will order themselves, bandits and robbers will be pacified by themselves, the achievement of restoration can be hoped for within ten days or a month, and the allotted span of the dynasty will be endless forever. I hope you will move according to the proper time and act in accord with what is right, turn the imperial carriage back to the upper capital, recreate the state, renew the many policies, serve the ancestral temple by repairing offerings and sacrifices, and visit the imperial tombs to exalt filial thought. Though your subject should fall and die, in death I would have no regret.
translations.idiomatic: When Ziyi heard of this, he attached a memorial to Zhang Chongguang, Vice Minister of War, as Zhang returned from his consolation mission, and submitted it, saying: Your subject has heard that the land of Yongzhou was called Heaven's storehouse in antiquity. To the right it reaches toward Long and Shu; to the left it controls Xiao and Han. Before it are the defenses of Zhongnan and Taihua; behind it are the fastnesses of the clear Wei and muddy Yellow River. It is a mysterious inner place of divine clarity and the capital of kings. The region extends several thousand li and has more than a hundred thousand armored troops; its soldiers are strong and its men brave, looking proudly over the eight directions. When there is advantage, it goes out to attack; when there is no advantage, it goes in to defend. This is a state for the use of arms and is not the same as the various lands of Xia. Qin and Han relied on it and in the end completed imperial enterprises. Afterward, some who occupied it were secure, and some who left it perished; what earlier histories record is not limited to one surname. By the end of the Sui house, Emperor Yang moved south, the Yellow River and Luo region became mounds and ruins, and wars arose. Gaozu raised the righteous standard and also first entered the Pass, and only then was able to cut down the treacherous heroes and settle the realm. Down to the flourishing of Taizong and Gaozong and the brightness of Zhongzong and Xuanzong, most dwelt in Qinchuan and few lived in Eastern Luo. Recently the Jie barbarian created disorder and the nine services split apart; Hebei and Henan all followed the rebel command. Yet the late emperor relied on the troops of Shuofang, and Qingxu fled in defeat; Your Majesty relied on the armies of the western lands, and Chaoyi was executed. This was not only the Way of Heaven assisting the obedient; it was also the terrain making it so. Your Majesty knows this, and it is not an embellished argument by your subject. Recently, because Tibet pressed and threatened us, the imperial carriage made an eastern tour. This was because the soldiers of the Six Armies had never been well trained; they were all men of the markets, butchers, and sellers of wine, intent on hanging up empty names and merely avoiding conscription and taxes. When driven into battle, not one in a hundred was fit. There were also those who secretly paid money and goods to seek exemption. In addition, eunuchs concealed matters and the many policies were much neglected. This caused Your Majesty to be shaken and unsettled and to withdraw to the region of Shaan. This all relates to appointments being misplaced. How can it be said that the Qin lands are not good? Now there is talk on the roads, and I do not know whether it is trustworthy, but all say Your Majesty already has a settled command and will visit the capital of Luo. Your subject has considered the matter carefully and has not seen its benefit. As for the land of Eastern Zhou, it has long been trapped among the rebels. Palaces and halls have been burned, and not one in ten survives. The hundred offices are desolate and abandoned, without even a foot of beam; in the imperial district between them, there are not a thousand households. Wells and settlements are choked with brush, jackals and wolves howl there, and there is neither military supply nor human strength. Eastward to Zheng and Bian, reaching to Xufang, and northward from Tanhuai, passing through the lands of Xiang, human smoke is cut off and a thousand li are bleak. How will it provide sacrificial animals and provisions for the imperial carriage, or supply lodgings for the hundred officials? Moreover, its territory is narrow, only a few hundred li across. To the east is Chenggao; to the south are the Two Peaks. Its terrain offers no reliable defense and merely makes a battlefield. How can Your Majesty abandon the position of long security, follow a policy of utmost danger, neglect the plan for the altars of state, and produce doubt in the hearts of the realm? Though your subject is extremely foolish, I privately do not choose this for Your Majesty. Moreover, what the sacred intent worries over is surely that the capital region has newly suffered plunder, the fields are empty, grain may not suffice, and state use may have shortages. From what your subject sees, I deeply think this is not so. Formerly Duke Wen of Wei was the ruler of a small state, only a lord among the feudal lords. After Duke Yi was destroyed by the Di, he first lodged at Cao, wore clothes of coarse cloth and a cap of plain silk; in his first year he had thirty war chariots, and by his last year three hundred, and in the end he was able to recover his old enterprise and enjoy boundless blessing. How much more a brilliant Son of Heaven: if you personally practice frugality and economize use, dismiss officials who eat without service, remove redundant food-consuming officers, suppress the power of Shudiao and Yiya, employ the uprightness of Qu Yuan and Shi Qiu, lighten levies and use strength carefully, show compassion to the distressed and reach even widowers, entrust the chief ministers with selecting the worthy and employing the able, and entrust the old minister with training troops and resisting insult, then the black-haired people will order themselves, bandits and robbers will be pacified by themselves, the achievement of restoration can be hoped for within ten days or a month, and the allotted span of the dynasty will be endless forever. I hope you will move according to the proper time and act in accord with what is right, turn the imperial carriage back to the upper capital, recreate the state, renew the many policies, serve the ancestral temple by repairing offerings and sacrifices, and visit the imperial tombs to exalt filial thought. Though your subject should fall and die, in death I would have no regret.

sentences.zh: 代宗省表，垂泣謂左右曰：「子儀用心，真社稷臣也。

translations.literal: Daizong read the memorial and, weeping, told those around him: "Ziyi's devotion makes him a true minister of the altars of state.
translations.idiomatic: Daizong read the memorial and, weeping, told those around him, "In his loyalty Ziyi is a true pillar of the realm.

sentences.zh: 可亟還京師。」

translations.literal: We may return to the capital at once."
translations.idiomatic: We should return to the capital at once."

sentences.zh: 十一月，車駕自陜還宮，子儀伏地請罪，帝駐車勞之曰：「朕用卿不早，故及於此。」

translations.literal: In the eleventh month the imperial carriage returned from Shan Prefecture to the palace; Ziyi prostrated himself and asked to be punished. The emperor stopped his carriage and consoled him, saying: "I did not employ you soon enough, and hence we came to this."
translations.idiomatic: In the eleventh month the emperor returned from Shan Prefecture to the palace. Ziyi prostrated himself and asked to be punished. The emperor halted his carriage and comforted him, saying, "I did not use you soon enough, and that is why this happened."

sentences.zh: 乃賜鐵券，圖形淩煙閣。

translations.literal: Thereupon he granted an iron certificate and had his likeness placed in Lingyan Pavilion.
translations.idiomatic: He then granted Ziyi an iron certificate of immunity and had his portrait placed in Lingyan Pavilion.

sentences.zh: 是時，河北副元帥僕固懷恩方頓軍汾州，掠并、汾諸縣以為己邑。

translations.literal: At this time the Hebei deputy supreme commander Pugu Huaien was encamped at Fen Prefecture, plundering the counties of Bing and Fen and treating them as his own territory.
translations.idiomatic: At this time Pugu Huaien, deputy supreme commander of Hebei, was encamped at Fen Prefecture, plundering the counties of Bing and Fen and treating them as his private domain.

sentences.zh: 乃以子儀兼關內河東副元帥、河中節度觀察使，出鎮河中。

translations.literal: Thereupon Ziyi was made concurrently deputy supreme commander of Guannei and Hedong and military governor and observation commissioner of Hezhong, and sent out to take command at Hezhong.
translations.idiomatic: The court then made Ziyi concurrently deputy supreme commander of Guannei and Hedong and military governor and observation commissioner of Hezhong, and sent him out to command from there.

sentences.zh: 蕃戎既退，僕固懷恩部下離散。

translations.literal: Once the barbarians of the west had withdrawn, the subordinates of Pugu Huaien dispersed.
translations.idiomatic: Once the western barbarians had withdrawn, Pugu Huaien's followers scattered.

sentences.zh: 是月，懷恩子瑒主兵榆次，為帳下將張惟嶽所殺，傳首京師。

translations.literal: That month Huaien's son Yang commanded troops at Yuci and was killed by his tent officer Zhang Weiyue; his head was sent to the capital.
translations.idiomatic: That month Huaien's son Yang held troops at Yuci and was killed by his officer Zhang Weiyue; his head was sent to the capital.

sentences.zh: 惟嶽以瑒之眾歸於子儀，懷恩懼，棄其母而走靈州。

translations.literal: Weiyue brought Yang's troops to submit to Ziyi; Huaien was afraid, abandoned his mother, and fled to Ling Prefecture.
translations.idiomatic: Weiyue brought Yang's troops over to Ziyi. Huaien, terrified, abandoned his mother and fled to Ling Prefecture.

sentences.zh: 明年九月，以子儀守太尉，充北道邠寧、涇原、河西已東通和蕃及朔方招撫觀察使，其關內河東副元帥、中書令如故。

translations.literal: In the ninth month of the following year Ziyi was appointed Grand Preceptor and made Northern Circuit pacification and observation commissioner for Binning, Jingyuan, and Hexi eastward, for communicating with and harmonizing the Tibetans, and for Shuofang; his posts as deputy supreme commander of Guannei and Hedong and as Grand Councilor remained as before.
translations.idiomatic: In the ninth month of the following year Ziyi was made Grand Preceptor and appointed northern-circuit pacification and observation commissioner over Binning, Jingyuan, Hexi eastward, and Shuofang, charged with managing relations with the Tibetans. His posts as deputy supreme commander of Guannei and Hedong and as grand councilor remained unchanged.

sentences.zh: 子儀以懷恩未誅，不宜讓使，堅辭太尉，曰：「太尉職雄任重，竊憂非據，輒敢上聞。

translations.literal: Because Huaien had not yet been executed, Ziyi held that it was not fitting to accept the commission; he firmly declined the Grand Preceptor's post, saying: "The office of Grand Preceptor is lofty and its burden heavy; I privately fear I am not equal to the post and venture to report this to Your Majesty.
translations.idiomatic: Because Huaien had not yet been brought to justice, Ziyi held that he ought not accept the appointment. He firmly declined the Grand Preceptor's post, saying, "The Grand Preceptor's office is exalted and its burden heavy. I fear I am unworthy of it and venture to lay this before Your Majesty.

sentences.zh: 伏奉詔書，未允誠懇。

translations.literal: Having received the imperial edict in submission, my sincere request was not granted.
translations.idiomatic: I have received Your Majesty's edict, yet my sincere request has not been granted.

sentences.zh: 臣疇昔之分，早知止足，今茲累請，竊懼滿盈。

translations.literal: Your subject's allotted portion from of old—I early knew when to stop; now, with these repeated requests, I privately fear overflowing fullness.
translations.idiomatic: Your subject has long known the limits of his proper share and when to stop. These repeated petitions come only from my fear of excess.

sentences.zh: 義實由衷，事非矯飾，志之所至，敢不盡言。

translations.literal: The righteousness is truly from the heart; the matter is not feigned ornament. Where my will reaches, how dare I not speak fully?
translations.idiomatic: This is sincere conviction, not pretense. Where my heart leads, how can I fail to speak plainly?

sentences.zh: 自兵亂已來，紀綱浸壞，時多躁競，俗少廉隅。

translations.literal: Since the military chaos began, regulations have gradually deteriorated; the age has much rash competition, and custom has little integrity.
translations.idiomatic: Since the wars began, discipline has steadily decayed. The age is full of reckless ambition, and integrity has grown rare.

sentences.zh: 德薄而位尊，功微而賞厚，實繁有眾，不可殫論。

translations.literal: Virtue is thin yet position is eminent; merit is slight yet reward is generous—such cases are indeed many and cannot be exhaustively discussed.
translations.idiomatic: Men of slight virtue hold lofty rank; men of slight merit receive lavish reward. Such cases are countless and cannot all be discussed.

sentences.zh: 臣每見之，深以為念。

translations.literal: Whenever your subject sees this, he deeply takes it to heart.
translations.idiomatic: Whenever I see this, it weighs heavily on my mind.

sentences.zh: 昔范宣子讓，其下皆讓，欒騕為汰，不敢違也。

translations.literal: Formerly, when Fan Xuanzi yielded, those beneath all yielded; though Luan Yan was dissolute, he did not dare defy it.
translations.idiomatic: In antiquity, when Fan Xuanzi yielded office, all beneath him yielded as well. Even Luan Yan, for all his excess, did not dare break that example.

sentences.zh: 臣誠薄劣，竊慕古人，務欲以身率先，大變浮俗，是用勤勤懇懇，願罷此官，庶禮讓興行，由臣而致也。

translations.literal: Your subject is truly base and inferior, yet privately admires the ancients and strives to lead by personal example and greatly transform floating custom; therefore I am diligent and earnest in wishing to resign this office, hoping that courtesy and yielding may arise and be achieved through me.
translations.idiomatic: I am a man of little worth, yet I admire the ancients and wish to lead by example and change these shallow ways. That is why I earnestly beg to be relieved of this office, so that courtesy and restraint may be restored through my act.

sentences.zh: 臣位為上相，爵為真王，參啟沃之謀，受腹心之寄，恩榮已極，功業已成，尋合乞骸，保全餘齒。

translations.literal: Your subject's rank is chief minister and his ennoblement is that of a full prince; I participate in counsel of utmost trust and have received the heart-and-belly entrustment. Grace and glory have already reached their limit, and my achievements are already complete—it is fitting soon to request retirement and preserve my remaining years.
translations.idiomatic: I stand as chief minister and hold the rank of a full prince. I share in the deepest counsel of state and bear the emperor's innermost trust. Honor has already reached its height, and my work is done. It is time to ask leave to retire and preserve what years remain to me.

sentences.zh: 但以冠仇在近，家國未安，臣子之心，不敢寧處。

translations.literal: Only because the crowned enemy is near at hand, the state and family are not yet secure—the heart of a subject and minister dares not dwell in ease.
translations.idiomatic: It is only that our mortal foe still presses close, the realm and house are not yet at peace, and the heart of a loyal subject cannot rest easy.

sentences.zh: 茍西戎即敘，懷恩就擒，疇昔官爵，誓無所受，必當追蹤范蠡，繼跡留侯。

translations.literal: If the Western Rong are at once pacified and Huai'en is captured and taken, the official ranks of former days I swear I shall not accept; I shall surely follow in the tracks of Fan Li and continue in the footsteps of the Marquis of Liu.
translations.idiomatic: Should the western tribes be brought to order and Huai'en taken prisoner, I swear I will accept none of the honors I once held. I mean to retire as Fan Li did, and walk the path of the Marquis of Liu.

sentences.zh: 臣之鄙懷，切在於此。」

translations.literal: Your subject's humble wish is urgently set upon this."
translations.idiomatic: This, and nothing else, is the humble wish I hold in my heart."

sentences.zh: 優詔不許。

translations.literal: An excellent edict did not permit it.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor issued a gracious edict refusing his request.

sentences.zh: 子儀見上，感泣懇讓，乃止。

translations.literal: Ziyi had an audience with the emperor, wept in gratitude and earnestly declined, and then stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi went before the throne, wept as he pleaded to be released from the honor, and at last desisted.

sentences.zh: 十月，僕固懷恩引吐蕃、回紇、党項數十萬南下，京師大恐，子儀出鎮奉天。

translations.literal: In the tenth month, Pugu Huai'en led several hundred thousand Tibetans, Uyghurs, and Tanguts southward; the capital was greatly terrified, and Ziyi went out to command at Fengtian.
translations.idiomatic: In the tenth month Pugu Huai'en marched south at the head of several hundred thousand Tibetans, Uyghurs, and Tangut warriors. Terror seized the capital, and Ziyi rode out to take command at Fengtian.

sentences.zh: 帝召子儀問禦戎之計，子儀曰：「以臣所見，懷恩無能為也。」

translations.literal: The emperor summoned Ziyi to ask about plans for repelling the barbarians. Ziyi said: "In your subject's view, Huai'en will not be able to accomplish anything."
translations.idiomatic: The emperor called Ziyi in to ask how the invaders might be repelled. Ziyi answered, "As I see it, Huai'en can do nothing."

sentences.zh: 帝問其故，對曰：「懷恩雖稱驍勇，素失士心，今所以能為亂者，引思歸之人耳。

translations.literal: The emperor asked the reason. He replied: "Although Huai'en is called brave and fierce, he has long lost the hearts of his soldiers; what enables him to make trouble now is only that he is leading men who long to return home.
translations.idiomatic: When the emperor asked why, he replied, "Huai'en may have a name for valor, but he lost his men's loyalty long ago. All that lets him raise rebellion is that he is dragging along troops who only want to go home.

sentences.zh: 懷恩本臣偏將，其下皆臣之部曲，臣恩信嘗及之，今臣為大將，必不忍以鋒刃相向，以此知其無能為也。」

translations.literal: Huai'en was originally your subject's junior general; those beneath him were all your subject's personal troops. Your subject's grace and trust once reached them. Now that your subject is the grand general, they surely cannot bear to turn blades against me—by this I know he will not be able to accomplish anything."
translations.idiomatic: Huai'en was once my subordinate, and his men were my own troops. They knew my kindness and trust. Now that I command the army, they will not willingly cross swords with me. That is how I know he can do nothing."

sentences.zh: 虜寇邠州，子儀在涇陽，子儀令長男朔方兵馬使曜率師援之，與邠寧節度使白孝德閉城拒守。

translations.literal: The barbarians raided Bin Prefecture. Ziyi was at Jingyang. Ziyi ordered his eldest son, the Shuofang army-and-horse commissioner Yao, to lead troops to reinforce it; together with the Binning military governor Bai Xiaode, they closed the city and held fast in defense.
translations.idiomatic: The enemy struck Bin Prefecture while Ziyi was at Jingyang. He sent his eldest son Guo Yao, military commissioner of Shuofang, to relieve the city. With Bai Xiaode, military governor of Binning, they shut the gates and stood firm.

sentences.zh: 懷恩前鋒至奉天，近城挑戰，諸將請擊之，子儀止之曰：「夫客兵深入，利在速戰，不可爭鋒。

translations.literal: Huai'en's vanguard reached Fengtian, drew near the city, and offered battle. The generals requested to attack, but Ziyi stopped them, saying: "An invading army that has penetrated deep gains advantage in quick battle—one must not contend at the spearpoint.
translations.idiomatic: Huai'en's advance guard reached Fengtian and challenged the walls. The officers wanted to strike, but Ziyi forbade it. "An enemy army deep in hostile country wants a quick fight," he said. "We must not meet them blade to blade.

sentences.zh: 彼皆吾之部曲，緩之自當攜貳；

translations.literal: They are all my former troops; if we take it slowly, they will naturally become divided in loyalty.
translations.idiomatic: Those men were once mine. Give them time, and they will split among themselves.

sentences.zh: 若迫之，是速其戰，戰則勝負未可知。

translations.literal: If we press them, we will hasten their battle; once they fight, victory and defeat cannot be known.
translations.idiomatic: Drive them hard and you force the battle—and then who can say who will win?

sentences.zh: 敢言戰者斬！」

translations.literal: Whoever dares speak of fighting shall be beheaded!"
translations.idiomatic: Let any man who dares speak of giving battle lose his head!"

sentences.zh: 堅壁待之，果不戰而退。

translations.literal: They fortified the walls and waited; sure enough, without fighting they withdrew.
translations.idiomatic: They held behind strong walls and waited. In the end the enemy withdrew without a fight.

sentences.zh: 子儀自涇陽入朝，帝御安福門待之，命子儀樓上行朝見之禮，宴賜隆厚。

translations.literal: Ziyi entered court from Jingyang. The emperor awaited him at Anfu Gate, ordered Ziyi to perform the court-audience rite from atop the gate tower, and bestowed a banquet with lavish gifts.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi came to court from Jingyang. The emperor received him at Anfu Gate, had him perform the audience ceremony from the gate tower, and honored him with a feast and rich rewards.

sentences.zh: 十一月，以子儀為尚書令，上表懇辭曰：「臣以薄劣，素乏行能，逢時擾攘，猥蒙驅策，內參朝政，外總兵權。

translations.literal: In the eleventh month, Ziyi was made Director of the Imperial Secretariat. He submitted a memorial earnestly declining: "Your subject, by virtue of my thin merit and inferior quality, has always lacked conduct and ability. Encountering a troubled age, I have undeservedly received driving command. Within I participate in court governance; without I hold overall military authority.
translations.idiomatic: In the eleventh month Ziyi was appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat. He memorialized the throne in earnest refusal: "I am a man of little talent and poor merit. In these turbulent times I have undeservedly been pressed into service, sharing in court policy within and commanding armies without.

sentences.zh: 上不能翼戴三光，下不能糾逖群慝，功微賞厚，任重恩深，覆餗之憂，實盈寤寐。

translations.literal: Above I cannot uphold the Three Luminaries; below I cannot rectify distant evils. My merit is slight yet my rewards are heavy; my burdens are great yet your grace is deep. The fear of overturning the pot truly fills my waking and sleeping hours.
translations.idiomatic: I cannot worthily serve heaven, earth, and the sovereign above, nor put down wickedness far and near below. My deeds are small while your gifts are great; my burden is heavy while your kindness runs deep. Night and day I live in dread of failing you.

sentences.zh: 臣昨所以固辭太尉，乞保餘年，殊私曲臨，遂見矜許。

translations.literal: Yesterday your subject, for this reason, firmly declined the post of Grand Commandant, begging to preserve my remaining years. Your extraordinary private kindness bent down to me, and I was thus granted permission.
translations.idiomatic: Only yesterday I firmly refused the Grand Commandant's seal and begged to keep what years remain to me. Your Majesty's gracious indulgence bent to my wish, and you were pleased to allow it.

sentences.zh: 竊謂陛下已知其願，深察其心，豈意未歷旬時，復延寵命。

translations.literal: I privately supposed Your Majesty already knew my wish and had deeply discerned my heart. How could I have expected that, before ten days had passed, you would again extend a favoring appointment?
translations.idiomatic: I had thought Your Majesty understood my wish and saw my heart clearly. I never imagined that in less than ten days you would honor me with a new appointment.

sentences.zh: 以臣褊淺，又寡智謀，安可謬職南宮，當茲大任？

translations.literal: Given my narrowness and shallowness, and my lack of wisdom and strategy, how could I wrongly occupy the Southern Palace post and bear this great responsibility?
translations.idiomatic: I am narrow-minded, shallow, and lacking in counsel. How can such a man rightly fill the office of the Secretariat and shoulder so great a charge?

sentences.zh: 況太宗昔居籓邸，嘗踐此官，累聖相承，曠而不置。

translations.literal: Moreover, when Taizong formerly resided in the princely residence, he once held this office. Successive sages have inherited it, and the post has long gone unfilled.
translations.idiomatic: Besides, when Emperor Taizong still lived in the princely residence he once held this office. Since then successive sage emperors have kept it vacant.

sentences.zh: 皇太子為雍王之日，陛下以其總兵薄伐，平定關東，飲至策勛，再有斯授。

translations.literal: When the Crown Prince was Prince of Yong, Your Majesty, because he had marshaled troops on a punitive expedition and pacified the eastern passes, at the ceremony of drinking to victory and recording merits, again received this appointment.
translations.idiomatic: When the Crown Prince was still Prince of Yong, Your Majesty gave him this post after he took command of a punitive campaign, pacified the eastern passes, and was honored at the victory feast for his deeds.

sentences.zh: 豈臣末職，敢亂大倫？

translations.literal: How could one of lowly rank like your subject dare disrupt the great order?
translations.idiomatic: How could a man of my humble station dare disturb so august a precedent?

sentences.zh: 德薄位尊，難逃天子之責；

translations.literal: My virtue is thin yet my position is exalted—hard to escape the Son of Heaven's reproach.
translations.idiomatic: Virtue too slight for so high a rank cannot escape the judgment of heaven's son.

sentences.zh: 負乘致冠，復速神明之誅。

translations.literal: Like a small beast bearing too heavy a load, I would again hasten divine punishment.
translations.idiomatic: To take on more than my strength can bear would only invite heaven's wrath upon me.

sentences.zh: 伏乞天慈，俯停新命。」

translations.literal: I humbly beg Heaven's mercy to bend and halt this new appointment."
translations.idiomatic: I humbly beg Your Majesty, in your heavenly kindness, to withdraw this new command."

sentences.zh: 答詔不允。

translations.literal: The reply edict did not accede.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor's written reply refused to grant his request.

sentences.zh: 翌日，敕所司令子儀於尚書省視事。

translations.literal: The next day, an edict ordered the responsible offices to have Ziyi assume duties at the Imperial Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: The following day an edict commanded the relevant offices to install Ziyi at the Secretariat to begin his duties.

sentences.zh: 詔宰相百僚送上，遣射生五百騎執戟翼從，自朝堂至省，賜教坊樂。

translations.literal: An edict ordered the chancellors and the hundred officials to escort him up; five hundred mounted archers bearing halberds were dispatched to flank and follow him from the court hall to the Secretariat, and music from the Music Bureau was granted.
translations.idiomatic: The court ordered the chief ministers and all officials to escort him in procession. Five hundred mounted archers with halberds rode in attendance from the hall of audience to the Secretariat, and musicians from the imperial Music Bureau were sent to honor the occasion.

sentences.zh: 子儀不受，復上表曰：臣伏以尚書令，武德之際，太宗為之，昨瀝懇上陳，請罷斯職；而陛下未垂亮察，務欲褒崇，區區微誠，益用惶懼。何則？太宗立極之主，聖德在人，自後因廢此官，永代作則。陛下守文繼體，固當奉而行之，豈可猥私老臣，隳厥成式，上掩陛下之德，下貽萬方之非。臣雖至愚，安敢輕受？況久經兵亂，僭賞者多，一人之身，兼官數四，朱紫同色，清濁不分，「爛羊」之謠，復聞聖代。臣頃觀其弊，思革其源，以逆寇猶存，未敢輕議。今元兇沮敗，計日成擒，中外無虞，妖氛漸息。此陛下作法之際，審官之時，固合始於老臣，化及班列。豈可輕為此舉，以亂國章？國章亂於上，則庶政隳於下，海內之政皆亂，則國家又安得永代而無患哉！陛下茍能從臣之言，俯察誠請，彼貪榮冒進者，亦將各讓其所兼之官，自然天下文明，百工式敘，太平之業，可得而復也。臣誠蒙鄙，識昧古今，志之所切，實在於此。

translations.literal: Ziyi would not accept and again submitted a memorial, saying: Your subject humbly submits that as for Director of the Department of State Affairs, in the Wude era Taizong held this office. Yesterday I poured out my earnestness and stated upward my request that this office be withdrawn, yet Your Majesty has not extended discerning understanding and is determined to praise and exalt me. My small sincerity is all the more fearful. Why? Taizong was the ruler who established the throne, and his sacred virtue remains among the people. After him this office was therefore abolished, making a model for all ages. Your Majesty preserves the pattern and succeeds to the body of rule, and naturally should uphold and practice it. How could you improperly favor an old minister, destroy that completed rule, above conceal Your Majesty's virtue, and below leave criticism to the myriad regions? Though your subject is extremely foolish, how would I dare accept it lightly? Moreover, after long years of war and disorder, many have been given excessive rewards. One person's body may hold three or four concurrent offices; vermilion and purple become the same color, purity and impurity are not distinguished, and the song of "rotten sheep" is heard again in a sacred age. Your subject recently observed this abuse and thought to reform its source, but because the rebel enemy still remained, I did not dare discuss it lightly. Now the chief villain has been defeated and will be captured within days, inside and outside there is no danger, and the monstrous miasma is gradually ending. This is the moment for Your Majesty to establish law and the time to examine offices. It surely should begin with the old minister, and the transformation should reach the ranks of officials. How can this act be made lightly and thereby disorder the state's regulations? If the state's regulations are disordered above, then the many policies collapse below. If governance within the seas is all disordered, then how can the state remain for all generations without trouble? If Your Majesty can follow your subject's words and look down to examine my sincere request, those who covet glory and recklessly advance will each yield the offices they concurrently hold. Naturally the realm will be bright and ordered, the hundred crafts will be properly arranged, and the enterprise of great peace can be restored. Your subject is truly ignorant and coarse, and his understanding is dark regarding ancient and present matters, but what my will urgently seeks lies truly in this.

sentences.zh: 手詔答曰：「優崇之命，所以報功；總領之司，期於賦政。卿入居臺鉉，出統戎旃，爰自先朝，累匡多難，靖群氛於海表，凝庶績於天階。敏事而寡言，居敬而行簡，人難其易，爾易其難。所以命掌六聯，首茲百辟，顧循時議，僉謂允諧。而屢拜封章，懇懷讓揖，守淳素之道，語政理之源，無待禮成，曲從德讓。宜宣示於外，編之史冊。」遣內侍魚朝恩傳詔，賜美人盧氏等六人、從者八人，並車服、帷帳、床蓐、珍玩之具。

translations.literal: The handwritten imperial edict replied, "The command of generous exaltation is to repay merit; the office of overall leadership is expected to assign and govern policy. You, sir, enter to occupy the ministerial seat and go out to command the war banners. From the former reign onward, you have repeatedly corrected many difficulties, pacified the various miasmas beyond the seas, and brought the many achievements together on the steps of Heaven. Quick in affairs and sparing of speech, dwelling in reverence and acting with simplicity, what others find easy is hard for them, and what is hard you make easy. For this reason I commanded you to take charge of the six offices and stand at the head of the hundred officials. Looking through current deliberation, all say it is fitting and harmonious. Yet you have repeatedly bowed with sealed memorials, sincerely cherishing yielding and deference, keeping to the Way of purity and plainness, and speaking of the source of political order. Without waiting for the ceremony to be completed, I bend to follow your virtuous yielding. This should be proclaimed outside and entered in the historical records." He sent the eunuch Yu Chao'en to convey the edict, and granted six beauties including Lady Lu, eight attendants, and also carriages and robes, curtains and tents, bedding, and precious playthings.

He sent the eunuch Yu Chao'en to convey the edict, and granted six beauties including Lady Lu, eight attendants, and also carriages and robes, curtains and tents, bedding, and precious playthings.

sentences.zh: 時蕃虜屢寇京畿，倚蒲、陜為內地，常以重兵鎮之。

translations.literal: At this time the barbarian raiders repeatedly attacked the capital region; relying on Pu and Shaan as inner territory, the court constantly stationed heavy troops there to garrison them.
translations.idiomatic: In those days the frontier tribes raided the capital region again and again. The court treated Pu and Shaan as inner lands and kept large garrisons there.

sentences.zh: 永泰元年五月，以子儀都統河南道節度行營，出鎮河中。

translations.literal: In the fifth month of the first year of Yongtai, Ziyi was made overall commander of the Henan Circuit defense mobile headquarters and went out to command at Hezhong.
translations.idiomatic: In the fifth month of the first year of Yongtai, Ziyi was appointed supreme commander of the Henan defense headquarters and took up his post at Hezhong.

sentences.zh: 八月，僕固懷恩誘吐蕃、回紇、党項、羌、渾、奴剌，山賊任敷、鄭庭、郝德、劉開元等三十餘萬南下，先發數萬人掠同州，期自華陰趨藍田，以扼南路，懷恩率重兵繼其後。

translations.literal: In the eighth month, Pugu Huai'en incited Tibet, Uyghur, Tangut, Qiang, Hun, and Nula tribes, together with mountain bandits Ren Fu, Zheng Ting, Hao De, Liu Kaiyuan, and others—over three hundred thousand in all—to march south. He first sent tens of thousands to plunder Tong Prefecture, intending to advance from Huayin toward Lantian to choke the southern route; Huai'en followed with heavy troops.
translations.idiomatic: In the eighth month Pugu Huai'en stirred up Tibetans, Uyghurs, Tanguts, Qiang, Hun, and Nula, along with mountain rebels Ren Fu, Zheng Ting, Hao De, Liu Kaiyuan, and others—more than three hundred thousand men in all—to march south. He sent tens of thousands ahead to ravage Tong Prefecture, planning to push from Huayin toward Lantian and cut the southern road, while he followed with the main army.

sentences.zh: 回紇、吐蕃自涇、邠、鳳翔數道寇京畿，掠奉天、醴泉。

translations.literal: Uyghurs and Tibetans from Jing, Bin, and Fengxiang by several routes invaded the capital region, plundering Fengtian and Liquan.
translations.idiomatic: Uyghur and Tibetan forces came down from Jing, Bin, and Fengxiang by several routes into the capital region, looting Fengtian and Liquan.

sentences.zh: 京師震恐，天子下詔親征，命李忠臣屯東渭橋，李光進屯雲陽，馬璘、郝廷玉屯便橋，駱奉先、李日越屯盩啡，李抱玉屯鳳翔。

translations.literal: The capital was shaken with terror. The Son of Heaven issued an edict for a personal campaign, ordering Li Zhongchen to encamp at East Wei Bridge, Li Guangjin at Yunyang, Ma Lin and Hao Tingyu at Bian Bridge, Luo Fengxian and Li Riyue at Zhouzhi, and Li Baoyu at Fengxiang.
translations.idiomatic: Terror seized the capital. The emperor proclaimed that he would take the field in person and ordered Li Zhongchen to hold East Wei Bridge, Li Guangjin Yunyang, Ma Lin and Hao Tingyu Bian Bridge, Luo Fengxian and Li Riyue Zhouzhi, and Li Baoyu Fengxiang.

sentences.zh: 周智光屯同州，杜冕屯坊州，天子以禁軍屯苑內。

translations.literal: Zhou Zhiguang encamped at Tong Prefecture, Du Mian at Fang Prefecture; the Son of Heaven stationed the palace guard within the park.
translations.idiomatic: Zhou Zhiguang took position at Tong Prefecture and Du Mian at Fang Prefecture, while the emperor kept the palace guard within the imperial park.

sentences.zh: 京城壯丁，並令團結。

translations.literal: Able-bodied men of the capital city were all ordered to form militia units.
translations.idiomatic: Every able-bodied man in the capital was ordered to muster for defense.

sentences.zh: 城二門塞其一。

translations.literal: Of the city's two gates, one was blocked shut.
translations.idiomatic: One of the city's two gates was sealed off.

sentences.zh: 魚朝恩括士庶私馬，重兵捉城門，市民由竇穴而遁去，人情危迫。

translations.literal: Yu Chao'en requisitioned private horses from gentry and commoners; heavily armed troops guarded the city gates, and townspeople fled through holes and burrows; popular sentiment was tense and desperate.
translations.idiomatic: Yu Chao'en seized private horses from nobles and commoners alike. Heavy detachments controlled the gates, and people slipped out through holes and crawl spaces. Fear and desperation spread through the city.

sentences.zh: 是時，急召子儀自河中至，屯於涇陽，而虜騎已合。

translations.literal: At this time Ziyi was urgently summoned from Hezhong; he encamped at Jingyang, but the barbarian cavalry had already united.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi was urgently recalled from Hezhong and took position at Jingyang, but the enemy horsemen had already joined forces.

sentences.zh: 子儀一軍萬餘人，而雜虜圍之數重。

translations.literal: Ziyi's single army numbered a little over ten thousand, yet the mixed barbarian forces surrounded them in several rings.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi had barely ten thousand men, while the mixed barbarian host closed around him in layer upon layer.

sentences.zh: 子儀使李國臣、高升拒其東，魏楚玉當其南，陳回光當其西，朱元琮當其北。

translations.literal: Ziyi sent Li Guochen and Gao Sheng to hold the east, Wei Chuyu the south, Chen Huiguang the west, and Zhu Yuancong the north.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi posted Li Guochen and Gao Sheng to the east, Wei Chuyu to the south, Chen Huiguang to the west, and Zhu Yuancong to the north.

sentences.zh: 子儀率甲騎二千出沒於左右前後，虜見而問：「此誰也？」

translations.literal: Ziyi personally led two thousand armored cavalry appearing and disappearing to left, right, front, and rear. The barbarians saw this and asked: "Who is this?"
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi himself led two thousand armored horsemen, riding out and wheeling back on every side. The enemy saw them and asked, "Who is that?"

sentences.zh: 報曰：「郭令公也。」

translations.literal: They were told: "It is Minister Guo."
translations.idiomatic: They were answered, "It is Minister Guo."

sentences.zh: 回紇曰：「令公存乎？

translations.literal: The Uyghurs said: "Is Minister Guo alive?
translations.idiomatic: The Uyghurs cried, "Is Minister Guo still alive?

sentences.zh: 僕固懷恩言天可汗已棄四海，令公亦謝世，中國無主，故從其來。

translations.literal: Pugu Huai'en said the Celestial Kaghan had abandoned the realm and Minister Guo had also passed from the world, and China had no ruler—therefore we came with him.
translations.idiomatic: Pugu Huai'en told us the Heavenly Kaghan had forsaken the empire, that Minister Guo was dead, and that China had no master. That is why we came with him.

sentences.zh: 今令公存，天可汗存乎？」

translations.literal: Now that Minister Guo lives, does the Celestial Kaghan live?"
translations.idiomatic: If Minister Guo lives, does the Heavenly Kaghan live as well?"

sentences.zh: 報之曰：「皇帝萬歲無疆。」

translations.literal: They were told: "The emperor is ten thousand years without limit."
translations.idiomatic: They were told, "The emperor endures—ten thousand years without end."

sentences.zh: 回紇皆曰：「懷恩欺我。」

translations.literal: The Huihe all said: 'Huai'en has deceived us.'
translations.idiomatic: The Uyghurs all cried out: "Huai'en has lied to us."

sentences.zh: 子儀又使諭之曰：「公等頃年遠涉萬里，翦除兇逆，恢復二京。

translations.literal: Ziyi again sent someone to instruct them, saying: 'You all, in recent years, traveled far ten thousand li, cut down the violent rebels, and recovered the Two Capitals.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi sent envoys again to reason with them: "Not long ago you crossed ten thousand li to crush the rebels and restore Chang'an and Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 是時子儀與公等周旋艱難，何日忘之。

translations.literal: At that time Ziyi and you all endured hardships together—when would one forget that?
translations.idiomatic: In those days Ziyi stood with you through every hardship—how could any of us forget?

sentences.zh: 今忽棄舊好，助一叛臣，何其愚也！

translations.literal: Now you suddenly abandon our old friendship to aid a rebellious minister—how foolish!
translations.idiomatic: Now you cast aside an old alliance to serve a traitor—what folly is this!

sentences.zh: 且懷恩背主棄親，於公等何有？」

translations.literal: Moreover, Huai'en betrayed his lord and abandoned his kin—what does he have to do with you all?'
translations.idiomatic: And Huai'en turned on his sovereign and forsook his own people—what is he to you?"

sentences.zh: 回紇曰：「謂令公亡矣，不然，何以至此。

translations.literal: The Huihe said: 'We thought the Lord Commanding General had died; otherwise, how could things have come to this?
translations.idiomatic: The Uyghurs answered: "We believed the Lord Commanding General was dead—otherwise how could matters have reached this pass?

sentences.zh: 令公誠存，安得而見之？」

translations.literal: If the Lord Commanding General truly still lives, how can we get to see him?'
translations.idiomatic: If he truly lives, how are we to see him?"

sentences.zh: 子儀將出，諸將諫曰：「戎狄之心，不可信也，請無往。」

translations.literal: As Ziyi was about to go out, the generals remonstrated, saying: 'The hearts of the barbarians cannot be trusted—please do not go.'
translations.idiomatic: When Ziyi prepared to go forth, his generals pleaded with him: "Barbarian hearts are not to be trusted—do not go."

sentences.zh: 子儀曰：「虜有數十倍之眾，今力固不敵，且至誠感神，況虜輩乎！」

translations.literal: Ziyi said: 'The enemy has forces many tens of times our number; our strength truly cannot match theirs—but utmost sincerity moves the gods, how much more these barbarian fellows!'
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi said: "They outnumber us tenfold; we cannot match them by force. Yet sincerity that moves heaven will surely move these men as well."

sentences.zh: 諸將曰：「請選鐵騎五百衛從。」

translations.literal: The generals said: 'Please select five hundred iron cavalry to guard and accompany you.'
translations.idiomatic: The generals said: "Let us choose five hundred armored horsemen to escort you."

sentences.zh: 子儀曰：「適足以為害也。」

translations.literal: Ziyi said: 'That would only be enough to cause harm.'
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi said: "That would only invite disaster."

sentences.zh: 乃傳呼曰：「令公來！」

translations.literal: He then had it announced: 'The Lord Commanding General has come!'
translations.idiomatic: Then he had his men call out: "The Lord Commanding General is here!"

sentences.zh: 虜初疑，持滿註矢以待之。

translations.literal: At first the barbarians were suspicious; they drew their bows full and nocked arrows to wait for him.
translations.idiomatic: At first the enemy doubted; they strung their bows and held arrows ready, waiting for him.

sentences.zh: 子儀以數十騎徐出，免胄而勞之曰：「安乎？

translations.literal: Ziyi came out slowly with several dozen horsemen, removed his helmet, and consoled them, saying: 'Are you well?
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi rode out slowly with a few dozen men, took off his helmet, and greeted them warmly: "Are you well?

sentences.zh: 久同忠義，何至於是？」

translations.literal: We have long shared loyalty and righteousness—how did it come to this?"
translations.idiomatic: We have long stood together in loyalty and righteousness—how did it come to this?"

sentences.zh: 回紇皆舍兵下馬齊拜曰：「果吾父也。」

translations.literal: The Huihe all laid down their weapons, dismounted, and bowed together, saying: 'Truly he is our father.'
translations.idiomatic: The Uyghurs all cast aside their weapons, dismounted, and bowed as one, crying: "It is truly our father!"

sentences.zh: 子儀召其首領，各飲之酒，與之羅錦，歡言如初。

translations.literal: Ziyi summoned their chieftains, had each drink wine, gave them silk brocades, and spoke joyfully as before.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi called their chieftains forward, shared wine with each, gave them brocades, and spoke with them as merrily as in old days.

sentences.zh: 子儀說回紇曰：「吐蕃本吾舅甥之國，無負而至，是無親也。

translations.literal: Ziyi persuaded the Huihe, saying: 'Tubo was originally our country linked by marriage ties of uncle and nephew; they have come without cause—that is being without kinship.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi urged the Uyghurs: "Tibet was once our kin by marriage; they have come against us without cause—that is to cast kinship aside.

sentences.zh: 若倒戈乘之，如拾地芥耳。

translations.literal: If you turn your spears and take advantage of them, it will be like picking up mustard seeds from the ground.
translations.idiomatic: If you turn your blades on them, victory will be like stooping to gather fallen seeds from the earth.

sentences.zh: 其羊馬滿野，長數百里，是謂天賜，不可失也。

translations.literal: Their sheep and horses fill the fields for several hundred li—this is what we call heaven's gift; it must not be missed.
translations.idiomatic: Their sheep and horses cover the plain for hundreds of li—a gift from heaven that must not be lost.

sentences.zh: 今能逐戎以利舉，與我繼好而凱旋，不亦善乎！」

translations.literal: If now you can drive off the barbarians for profit and renew friendship with me and return in triumph—would that not be good!"
translations.idiomatic: Drive off the barbarians for gain, renew our friendship, and return in triumph—is that not the better course?"

sentences.zh: 會懷恩暴死於鳴沙，群虜無所統攝，遂許諾，乃遣首領石野那等入朝。

translations.literal: Just then Huai'en died suddenly at Mingsha; the barbarian hosts had no one to command them, so they agreed, and sent chieftains including Shiyena and others to court.
translations.idiomatic: Just then Huai'en died suddenly at Mingsha; the tribes had no leader, and so they consented, sending chieftains such as Shiyena to pay court.

sentences.zh: 子儀遣朔方兵馬使白元光與回紇會軍。

translations.literal: Ziyi dispatched the Shuofang military commissioner Bai Yuanguang to join forces with the Huihe.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi sent the Shuofang military commissioner Bai Yuanguang to join the Uyghur army.

sentences.zh: 吐蕃知其謀，是夜奔退。

translations.literal: Tubo learned of their plan and that night fled in retreat.
translations.idiomatic: The Tibetans learned of the plot and fled that same night.

sentences.zh: 回紇與元光追之，子儀大軍繼其後，大破吐蕃十餘萬於靈武臺西原，斬首五萬，生擒萬人，收其所掠士女四千人，獲牛羊駝馬，三百里內不絕。

translations.literal: The Huihe and Yuanguang pursued them; Ziyi's great army followed after, and they routed over a hundred thousand Tibetans on the western plain of Lingwu Terrace, beheading fifty thousand, capturing ten thousand alive, recovering four thousand men and women they had seized, and taking sheep, cattle, camels, and horses in an unbroken line for three hundred li.
translations.idiomatic: The Uyghurs and Yuanguang gave chase; Ziyi's main force followed. On the western plain below Lingwu Terrace they shattered more than a hundred thousand Tibetans, took fifty thousand heads, captured ten thousand alive, recovered four thousand men and women the enemy had seized, and seized sheep, cattle, camels, and horses stretching unbroken for three hundred li.

sentences.zh: 子儀自涇陽入朝，加實封二百戶，還鎮河中。

translations.literal: Ziyi entered court from Jingyang, was granted two hundred additional enfeoffed households in actuality, and returned to garrison Hezhong.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi came to court from Jingyang, received two hundred additional households of actual enfeoffment, and returned to his post at Hezhong.

sentences.zh: 十二月，華州節度使周智光殺監軍張志斌謀叛，帝以同、華路阻，召子儀女婿工部侍郎趙縱受口詔往河中，令子儀起軍討之。

translations.literal: In the twelfth month, the Huazhou military commissioner Zhou Zhiguang killed the army supervisor Zhang Zhibin and plotted rebellion; because the Tong-Hua route was blocked, the Emperor summoned Ziyi's son-in-law, Ministry of Works Vice Minister Zhao Zong, to receive an oral edict and go to Hezhong, ordering Ziyi to raise troops and suppress him.
translations.idiomatic: In the twelfth month, the Huazhou military commissioner Zhou Zhiguang killed the army supervisor Zhang Zhibin and plotted rebellion. Because the road through Tong and Hua was cut off, the Emperor summoned Ziyi's son-in-law, Vice Minister of Works Zhao Zong, to receive an oral edict and go to Hezhong, commanding Ziyi to raise an army against him.

sentences.zh: 縱請為蠟書，令家僮間道賜子儀。

translations.literal: Zong requested a wax-sealed letter, and had household servants take a secret path to deliver it to Ziyi.
translations.idiomatic: Zong asked for a sealed letter in wax and sent a household servant by hidden route to deliver it to Ziyi.

sentences.zh: 奉詔大閱軍戎，將發，同華將吏聞軍起，乃斬智光父子，傳首京師。

translations.literal: Obeying the edict, he greatly reviewed the army and was about to depart; when the Tong-Hua officers heard the army was mobilizing, they beheaded Zhiguang and his son and sent their heads to the capital.
translations.idiomatic: Obeying the edict, he mustered his forces and prepared to march; when the officers of Tong and Hua heard the army was rising, they executed Zhiguang and his son and sent their heads to the capital.

sentences.zh: 二年二月，子儀入朝，宰相元載、王縉、僕射裴冕、京兆尹黎幹、內侍魚朝恩共出錢三十萬，置宴於子儀第，恩出羅錦二百匹，為子儀纏頭之費，極歡而罷。

translations.literal: In the second year, second month, Ziyi entered court; the chancellor Yuan Zai, Wang Jin, the Pushe Pei Mian, the Jingzhao Prefect Li Gan, and the inner attendant Yu Chao'en together contributed three hundred thousand, and held a banquet at Ziyi's residence; Chao'en contributed two hundred bolts of silk brocade as funds for Ziyi's head-wrapping celebration; they parted in utmost joy.
translations.idiomatic: In the second year, second month, Ziyi came to court. The chancellors Yuan Zai and Wang Jin, the Pushe Pei Mian, the Jingzhao prefect Li Gan, and the eunuch Yu Chao'en together contributed three hundred thousand cash and held a feast at Ziyi's mansion. Chao'en gave two hundred bolts of brocade as a gift for Ziyi's birthday celebration. They parted in the highest spirits.

sentences.zh: 九月，吐蕃寇涇州，詔子儀以步騎三萬自河中移屯涇陽。

translations.literal: In the ninth month, Tibetans invaded Jing Prefecture; an edict ordered Ziyi to move thirty thousand infantry and cavalry from Hezhong to encamp at Jingyang.
translations.idiomatic: In the ninth month, Tibetans raided Jing Prefecture. An edict ordered Ziyi to move thirty thousand foot and horse soldiers from Hezhong to camp at Jingyang.

sentences.zh: 十月，蕃軍退至靈州，邀擊敗之，斬馘二萬。

translations.literal: In the tenth month, the Tibetan army retreated to Ling Prefecture; they intercepted and defeated them, beheading twenty thousand.
translations.idiomatic: In the tenth month, the Tibetan army withdrew toward Ling Prefecture; Ziyi's forces intercepted and defeated them, taking twenty thousand heads.

sentences.zh: 十二月，盜發子儀父墓，捕盜未獲。

translations.literal: In the twelfth month, thieves opened Ziyi's father's tomb; the thieves were not captured.
translations.idiomatic: In the twelfth month, robbers desecrated the tomb of Ziyi's father; the culprits were never caught.

sentences.zh: 人以魚朝恩素惡子儀，疑其使之。

translations.literal: People, knowing Yu Chao'en had long hated Ziyi, suspected that he had someone do it.
translations.idiomatic: Because Yu Chao'en had long borne ill will toward Ziyi, many suspected he had arranged it.

sentences.zh: 子儀心知其故，及自涇陽將入，議者慮其構變，公卿憂之。

translations.literal: Ziyi knew in his heart the reason; when he was about to enter from Jingyang, those discussing affairs feared he might engineer a mutiny, and the ministers were worried.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi knew the truth in his heart. As he prepared to return from Jingyang, court gossips feared he might raise a rebellion, and the high ministers were deeply uneasy.

sentences.zh: 及子儀入見，帝言之，子儀號泣奏曰：「臣久主兵，不能禁暴，軍士殘人之墓，固亦多矣。

translations.literal: When Ziyi entered and was received by the Emperor, the Emperor spoke of it; Ziyi wailed and memorialized, saying: 'Your servant has long commanded troops and could not restrain violence; soldiers desecrating people's tombs—there have indeed been many.
translations.idiomatic: When Ziyi came before the Emperor, the Emperor spoke of the matter. Ziyi wept aloud and memorialized: "Your servant has long held command and failed to restrain his men's violence. Soldiers have desecrated graves before—this is hardly the first.

sentences.zh: 此臣不忠不孝，上獲天譴，非人患也。」

translations.literal: This is your servant's disloyalty and unfiliality; above, heaven's punishment was received—it is not a human misfortune."
translations.idiomatic: This is my own disloyalty and unfilial conduct. Heaven has punished me—it is no man's doing."

sentences.zh: 朝廷乃安。

translations.literal: The court then was reassured.
translations.idiomatic: The court was reassured.

sentences.zh: 三年三月，還河中。

translations.literal: Third year, third month: he returned to Hezhong.
translations.idiomatic: In the third year, third month, he returned to Hezhong.

sentences.zh: 八月，吐蕃寇靈武。

translations.literal: Eighth month: Tibetans invaded Lingwu.
translations.idiomatic: In the eighth month, Tibetans raided Lingwu.

sentences.zh: 九月，詔子儀率師五萬自河中移鎮奉天。

translations.literal: Ninth month: an edict ordered Ziyi to lead fifty thousand troops from Hezhong to relocate and garrison Fengtian.
translations.idiomatic: In the ninth month, an edict ordered Ziyi to lead fifty thousand men from Hezhong to take up command at Fengtian.

sentences.zh: 是月，白元光大破吐蕃靈武。

translations.literal: That month, Bai Yuanguang greatly defeated the Tibetans at Lingwu.
translations.idiomatic: That same month, Bai Yuanguang won a great victory over the Tibetans at Lingwu.

sentences.zh: 十月，子儀入朝，還鎮河中。

translations.literal: Tenth month: Ziyi entered court and returned to garrison Hezhong.
translations.idiomatic: In the tenth month, Ziyi came to court and returned to garrison Hezhong.

sentences.zh: 時議以西蕃侵寇，京師不安，馬璘雖在邠州，力不能拒，乃以子儀兼邠寧慶節度，自河中移鎮邠州，徙馬璘為涇原節度使。

translations.literal: At the time it was discussed that because the western Tibetans were invading and the capital was unsettled, though Ma Lin was at Bin Prefecture his strength could not resist them; therefore Ziyi was made concurrent Bin-Ning-Qing military commissioner, moved from Hezhong to garrison Bin Prefecture, and Ma Lin was transferred to be Jingyuan military commissioner.
translations.idiomatic: At the time, with western Tibetans pressing the frontier and the capital unsettled, Ma Lin at Bin Prefecture lacked the strength to hold them off. Ziyi was therefore made concurrent military commissioner of Bin, Ning, and Qing, moved from Hezhong to command at Bin Prefecture, and Ma Lin was transferred to Jingyuan.

sentences.zh: 八年十月，吐蕃寇涇州，子儀遣先鋒兵馬使渾瑊逆戰於宜祿，不利。

translations.literal: Year eight, tenth month: Tibetans invaded Jing Prefecture; Ziyi dispatched advance cavalry commander Hun Jian to meet them in battle at Yilu—unfavorable outcome.
translations.idiomatic: In the eighth year, tenth month, Tibetans attacked Jing Prefecture. Ziyi sent his advance cavalry commander Hun Jian to meet them at Yilu; the battle went against him.

sentences.zh: 會馬璘設伏於潘源，與瑊合擊，大破蕃軍，俘斬數萬計。

translations.literal: When Ma Lin set an ambush at Panyuan and joined with Jian in a combined attack, they greatly routed the Tibetan army, capturing and beheading tens of thousands.
translations.idiomatic: Then Ma Lin laid an ambush at Panyuan and joined Hun Jian in a combined strike, crushing the Tibetan army and capturing or killing tens of thousands.

sentences.zh: 回紇赤心賣馬一萬匹，有司以國計不充，請市千匹。

translations.literal: The Huihe chieftain Chixin offered ten thousand horses for sale; the relevant offices, because state finances were insufficient, requested buying only one thousand.
translations.idiomatic: The Uyghur chieftain Chixin offered ten thousand horses for sale; the relevant offices, finding the treasury insufficient, proposed buying only one thousand.

sentences.zh: 子儀以回紇前後立功，不宜阻意，請自納一年奉物，充回紇馬價，雖詔旨不允，內外稱之。

translations.literal: Ziyi, because the Huihe had repeatedly rendered meritorious service, felt their wishes should not be obstructed; he requested to pay out of his own one year's stipend gifts to cover the price of the Huihe horses; though the imperial edict did not approve, inside and outside all praised him.
translations.idiomatic: Ziyi, holding that the Uyghurs had repeatedly served the dynasty well and should not be refused, asked to pay from his own year's stipend to cover the full price of the horses. Though the throne did not grant his request, court and country alike praised him.

sentences.zh: 九年，入朝，代宗召對延英。

translations.literal: Year nine: he entered court; Emperor Daizong summoned him for audience in the Yanying Hall.
translations.idiomatic: In the ninth year he came to court; Emperor Daizong received him in audience at the Yanying Hall.

sentences.zh: 語及西蕃棄斥，苦戰不暇，言發涕零。

translations.literal: When they spoke of the western Tibetans being cast out and rejected, fighting bitterly without respite, as he spoke tears streamed down.
translations.idiomatic: When talk turned to the western Tibetans harrying the borders and the endless bitter fighting, tears fell as he spoke.

sentences.zh: 既退，復上封論備吐蕃利害，曰：朔方，國之北門，西禦犬戎，北虞獫狁，五城相去三千餘里。開元、天寶中，戰士十萬，戰馬三萬，才敵一隅。自先皇帝龍飛靈武，戰士從陛下收復兩京，東西南北，曾無寧歲。中年以僕固之役，又經耗散，人亡三分之二，比於天寶中有十分之一。今吐蕃充斥，勢強十倍，兼河、隴之地，雜羌、渾之眾，每歲來窺近郊。以朔方減十倍之軍，當吐蕃加十倍之騎，欲求制勝，豈易為力！入近內地，稱四節度，每將盈萬，每賊兼乘數四。臣所統將士，不當賊四分之一，所有征馬，不當賊百分之二，誠合固守，不宜與戰。又得馬璘牒，賊擬涉渭而南。臣若堅壁，恐犯畿甸；若過畿內，則國人大恐，諸道易搖。外有吐蕃之強，中有易搖之眾，外畏內懼，將何以安？臣伏以陛下橫制勝之術，力非不足，但慮簡練未精，進退未一，時淹師老，地闊勢分。願陛下更詢讜議，慎擇名將，俾之統軍，於諸道各抽精卒，成四五萬，則制勝之道必矣，未可失時。臣又料河南、河北、山南、江淮小鎮數千，大鎮數萬，空耗月餼，曾不習戰。臣請抽赴關中，教之戰陣，則軍聲益振，攻守必全，亦長久之計也。臣猥蒙任遇，垂二十年，今齒發已衰，願避賢路，止足不誡，神明所鑒。

translations.literal: After he withdrew, he again submitted a sealed memorial discussing the advantages and dangers of preparing against Tibet, saying: Shuofang is the state's northern gate; to the west it defends against the Quanrong, and to the north it guards against the Xianyun. The five cities are more than three thousand li apart. During the Kaiyuan and Tianbao eras, one hundred thousand fighting men and thirty thousand warhorses were barely enough to confront one corner. Since the late emperor rose like a dragon at Lingwu, the soldiers followed Your Majesty in recovering the two capitals, and east, west, south, and north, there has never been a peaceful year. In mid-course, with the Pugu campaign, they were again consumed and scattered; two thirds of the men are gone, and compared with the Tianbao era there remains one tenth. Now Tibet fills the region, its power ten times stronger, and it also possesses the lands of He and Long and mixes in the forces of the Qiang and Hun. Every year it comes to peer toward the near suburbs. To use the army of Shuofang, reduced tenfold, to face Tibetan cavalry increased tenfold, and hope to control victory: how could that be easy to do? Entering the nearby inner lands, they are called four military governorships; each command has more than ten thousand men, and each enemy fighter has several mounts. The officers and men commanded by your subject do not equal one fourth of the enemy, and the campaign horses we possess do not equal two percent of the enemy's. Truly, we should hold firm in defense and should not fight them. I have also received Ma Lin's dispatch saying that the enemy plans to cross the Wei and move south. If your subject holds fast behind walls, I fear they will violate the capital region; if they pass through the capital district, then the people of the state will be greatly frightened and the circuits will easily waver. Outside there is the strength of Tibet, and inside there are masses easily shaken. With fear outside and dread inside, how will stability be achieved? Your subject humbly thinks that Your Majesty's art for controlling victory is certainly not insufficient in strength; I only worry that selection and training are not yet refined, advance and retreat are not unified, time will delay the army and make it old, and the land is broad while the strategic position is divided. May Your Majesty further consult forthright advice, carefully select famous generals, have them command armies, and draw elite soldiers from each circuit to make forty or fifty thousand men. Then the way to control victory will be certain, and the moment must not be lost. Your subject also estimates that the small garrisons in Henan, Hebei, Shannan, and Jiang-Huai number in the thousands, and the large garrisons in the tens of thousands; they waste monthly rations and have never practiced battle. Your subject asks that they be drawn to Guanzhong and taught battle formations. Then the army's reputation will be further strengthened, attack and defense will both be complete, and this too will be a long-term plan. Your subject has unworthily received appointment and favor for nearly twenty years. Now my teeth and hair have already declined, and I wish to withdraw from the road of the worthy. Whether I know when to stop and be content is something the spirits will judge.
